data.title: Why bond investors quickly lost their enthusiasm for weak jobs figures
data.description:
By Isabel Wang and Christine Idzelis

A weak jobs report briefly saw U.S. debt rally, but yields climbed back as investors worried inflation could stay hot if the Fed hikes less

Bad news finally worked in Treasurys' favor - but just for a little while.

A weak U.S. jobs report did what bad news hadn't done in a while: It made U.S. debt look like a safe haven again - albeit briefly.

U.S. Treasurys gave up an early rally on Friday after a weaker-than-expected jobs report initially sent investors rushing into government debt.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury note BX:TMUBMUSD10Y fell 8 basis points to 5.155%, before reversing the move by midday trading. The policy-sensitive 2-year yield BX:TMUBMUSD02Y erased an 8.4-basis-point drop and turned sharply higher to 4.820%, according to FactSet data. Bond yields and prices move in the opposite direction to each other.

Data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed that U.S. employers added 29,000 jobs in September, which was well below expectations. The unemployment rate also ticked higher to 4.2%.

"Friday's cool jobs report doesn't guarantee lower yields, because the underlying drivers - inflation and sky-high government debt - are not going anywhere," said Nic Puckrin, macro and cross-asset analyst and founder of the Coin Bureau. "That means Americans must prepare for the double whammy of higher unemployment and rising prices at the store and at the pump, right in time for the winter holidays."

Treasury yields had a "knee-jerk" reaction lower after Friday's employment report showed the pace of jobs growth was cooler than economists expected.

Still, the economy is doing "fine," Chris Galipeau, head market strategist at the Franklin Templeton Institute, told MarketWatch. His view is that the 10-year yield's recent climb above 5% comes from "real economic growth," rather than long-term inflation fears.

To be sure, the weaker-than-expected jobs report wasn't the only force at work to push Treasury yields sharply lower early Friday. Yields surged in the third quarter, and some investors considered Treasurys to be oversold heading into Friday's session. Portfolio rebalancing at the start of the new quarter may have steered some capital back into beaten-down Treasurys, helping fixed income catch a brief bid.

Yet the jobs report didn't change the big-picture issues facing the Federal Reserve: Inflation remains a concern, the energy shock from the Iran war still is playing out globally, and traders still expect more interest-rate hikes from the central bank.

Fed-funds futures on Friday suggested an October hike looks unlikely. However, there was almost an 87% chance that the Fed would raise its benchmark rate in December by at least a quarter of a percentage point, from its current target range of 3.75% to 4%, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.

"The data helped ease a bit of the pressure on the Fed to keep a hiking cycle in place, and now we can sit back and let the market determine risk on its own without the Fed having to get involved in setting the overnight rate higher for the time being," said Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management.

That also explains why stocks were holding their ground despite the leg higher in Treasury yields, Mulberry told MarketWatch via phone on Friday.

"Equities can go higher while the 10-year Treasury goes higher because the fundamentals of the economy are still reasonably strong," he said.

The uptick in Treasury yields also came as oil prices (CL00) (BRN00) bounced from their session lows, erasing most of their earlier losses and underscoring how quickly inflation concerns can resurface.

U.S. stocks were higher Friday afternoon, with the Nasdaq Composite COMP up 1.2%, the S&P 500 SPX up 0.7% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA 0.4% higher, according to FactSet data.

-Isabel Wang -Christine Idzelis

data.title: US FDA closes lettuce parasite probe, links outbreak to Mexico facility
data.description:
The US FDA said on Friday it has concluded its investigation into a summer parasite outbreak, linking the illnesses to recalled shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico.

While investigators could not definitively determine how the contamination happened, tests confirmed the Cyclospora parasite was present in the environment where the lettuce was grown and processed, the health regulator said.

Patient illness reports and supply-chain tracking strongly supported the link between the recalled lettuce and the multistate outbreak, which causes intestinal sickness, it said.

After the probe concluded, the US Food and Drug Administration announced a 10-point plan to prevent similar outbreaks ahead of the 2027 growing season.

data.title: Bayer to Invest $2.2 Billion in U.S. Pharma Manufacturing Expansion
data.description:
By Adria Calatayud

Bayer said it plans to spend $2.2 billion to build a new manufacturing site in Ohio for its pharmaceutical business, becoming the latest European drugmaker to invest in the U.S.

The German agricultural and pharmaceutical group said Friday that its new site in New Albany will create around 600 jobs, with plans to open a first module dedicated to drug substance manufacturing in 2031, followed by a second module for finished products in 2034.

Bayer's pharma business has been looking to expand in the U.S., betting that an enlarged presence in the world's largest drug market can help it revive sales growth after two key products went off patent.

With the move, the company joins a growing list of European pharma companies committing to invest in the U.S. Under pressure from the Trump administration's tariff threats, big drugmakers like AstraZeneca, Novartis and Roche, as well as smaller rivals, pledged to make multibillion-dollar investments in the country and have started to execute their plans.

"The U.S. is our largest and fastest-growing market," Bayer's U.S. president, Sebastian Guth, said in an interview.

Stefan Oelrich, the president of Bayer's pharma division, told The Wall Street Journal earlier this year that the company was looking at expanding its U.S. manufacturing footprint to aid its turnaround plan.

Guth, who is also global chief operating officer of Bayer's pharma unit, said the company aims to bring manufacturing closer to its largest markets. The U.S. investment will also help the business accelerate growth momentum, one of its current priorities alongside strengthening its drug pipeline and boosting productivity, he added.

Bayer's Ohio site will initially focus on producing small-molecule oncology, cardiovascular and renal drugs, Guth said. The company also has a manufacturing site dedicated to biologic medicines--those grown from living cells--in Berkeley, Calif.

The group decided to invest in the U.S. partly because of the country's willingness to pay for innovation, Guth said.

data.title: Fidelity Sets $100 Million Asset Minimum for RIAs, Forcing Small Advisors to Move or Expand — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Andrew Welsch

Fidelity Investments is setting a new $100 million minimum asset level for registered investment advisors who want to use the company's trading and custody platform. The move may spur RIAs to move assets held at other custodians to Fidelity. Or, it could spark an exodus of small RIAs from Fidelity and a scramble among competing custodians to win their business.

Fidelity is the industry's second-largest custodian after Charles Schwab, providing RIAs with a trading platform and technology. It also safeguards client assets on behalf of RIAs.

A spokeswoman for Fidelity confirms that the Boston-based company will require existing RIA clients to maintain at least $100 million in assets on its custody platform. RIAs have until the end of June next year to meet the new requirement.

"We recognize that change requires thoughtful planning, and Fidelity has committed to providing firms with time to evaluate their options," the spokeswoman says.

RIAs new to Fidelity's platform were already required to meet the $100 million threshold, she says

RIAs don't frequently change custodians because the process can involve a lot of paperwork to move client accounts and assets, which requires approval from the client. Some RIAs, particularly ones with large assets under management, use more than one custodian.

Schwab says it has no asset minimum for RIAs and serves 11,000 advisory firms that have less than $100 million in assets under management. Last year, more than 65% of new state registrations chose Schwab as their custodian, according to Jon Beatty, head of Advisor Services at Schwab. "Small RIAs are the backbone of the independent advisory profession, and they always have been," Beatty says. "Whether an advisor is just launching a firm or managing billions, our role is the same: help them grow, compete, and succeed."

Although Fidelity and Schwab dominate the custody sector, they have been facing competition in recent years from new entrants trying to win market share. Their smaller competitors include investment bank Goldman Sachs, robo-advisor Betterment, and fintech startup Altruist, which recently agreed to sell itself to giant asset manager Vanguard. Some of them aren't hesitating to try to pick up business from small RIAs on Fidelity's platform.

Devon Klumb, director of sales at Betterment's RIA custody business, invited advisors to check out his company's offering in response to Fidelity's higher minimum.

"For what it's worth, we don't have minimums at Betterment Advisor Solutions, and the platform automates most of your portfolio management and back-office work," he wrote in a LinkedIn post. "What I love most about what we've built here is that we can (and want) to serve a firm well at any size."

data.title: Rate Hike Bets Have Substantially Dropped As Fed's Jefferson And Williams' Speeches Grant Confidence
data.description:
Key points:
  • Investor odds of a rate hike at the late-October meeting tumbled from 70% to around 25% after public remarks by Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams. 
  • Fed leadership stressed the importance of evaluating incoming economic indicators rather than rushing into consecutive rate increases, even as overall inflation remains elevated. 
  • While Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has stepped back from traditional forward guidance, major market participants interpreted the separate speeches as an authoritative signal to recalibrate policy forecasts. 

Top Federal Reserve officials signaled this week that the central bank is in no rush to lift borrowing costs at its upcoming policy meeting, prompting financial markets to abruptly dial back bets on another immediate interest rate hike.

Public addresses by Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams conveyed a shared belief that policymakers have ample room to evaluate economic indicators before considering further policy tightening.

The remarks successfully reined in Wall Street's expectations for a rate increase later this month, illustrating that market participants remain highly attentive to messaging from key central bank leaders.

Market Odds Shift Dramatically

Ahead of Williams's remarks early in the week, federal funds futures pricing indicated a 70% probability of a rate increase at the central bank's Oct. 27-28 meeting. By the time Jefferson concluded his address two days later—supported in part by cooler-than-anticipated inflation readings—those odds plummeted to roughly 25%.

According to the CME FedWatch tool, traders are factoring in a 22% probability, as of Oct. 3, of a Fed hike in October, down from 64% a week earlier.

Financial analysts viewed the speeches as a deliberate recalibration after traders drove up yields and aggressively priced in back-to-back policy tightening following the central bank's Sept. 16 rate hike.

Economists at Goldman Sachs noted that the combined messaging effectively solidified the case against an October hike. Similarly, Krishna Guha, head of economics at Evercore ISI, described the joint impact of the speeches as authoritative, as per Bloomberg, while JPMorgan Chase & Co. Chief U.S. Economist Michael Feroli noted that officials were reinforcing the idea that rate hikes do not need to occur at every consecutive meeting.

A New Era For Guidance

The central bank's recent policy actions mark a shift in how it communicates monetary policy. Last month, policymakers voted unanimously to raise benchmark interest rates by a quarter percentage point—marking the first increase since 2023—to combat persistent inflationary pressure and an accelerating economy. Projections issued alongside that decision indicated support for one additional rate move before year-end.

However, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has deliberately moved away from providing explicit forward guidance regarding future rate decisions. Warsh abstains from quarterly rate projections and avoids signaling upcoming moves in public forums, instead directing investors' focus strictly to incoming economic data.

Diverging Views Among Policymakers

The broader debate within the Federal Reserve reflects a complex economic backdrop, where consumer spending remains resilient, and overall growth appears robust despite recent cool-downs in employment and inflation metrics.

While several regional Fed presidents refrained from providing policy hints during a recent conference in Asheville, North Carolina, other key voices echoed a cautious stance. Fed Governor Michelle Bowman suggested there is little immediate urgency to adjust borrowing costs further.

Conversely, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said further rate increases may still be needed to bring inflation back to the 2% target, though she acknowledged that recent surges in longer-term bond yields could also help dampen economic activity.

At the time of writing, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the S&P 500 index, was up 0.8%; the Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (QQQ) jumped 1%; while the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) gained 0.4%.

data.title: Nike's 8% Drop Shows Investors Are Running Out of Patience
data.description:
Nike Inc. (NKE, Financials), the sportswear company attempting a multiyear turnaround under CEO Elliott Hill, is asking investors for more patience after another disappointing outlook pushed its shares down about 8% Friday.

Nike forecast steeper-than-expected declines in sales and profit for the fiscal year ending in May 2028 and announced another round of job cuts. Shares fell to about $32.22, near their lowest level in 12 years.

The bigger concern is how long the recovery could take. Nike said most savings from its restructuring will not arrive until fiscal 2029 and 2030.

Meanwhile, several of its largest businesses remain under pressure. Sportswear, China and the Jordan brand together account for more than half of company sales.

Hill has been rebuilding wholesale relationships, shifting product development back toward sports and simplifying operations. But revenue continues to decline across both wholesale and direct channels.

Jordan illustrates the challenge. Nike is reducing retro sneaker releases after oversupply and discounting weakened the franchise's premium positioning. China may require even more patience, with Hill saying stabilization could take multiple seasons and pressure profitability.

That leaves Nike's Nov. 16-17 investor day as a critical test, when investors will be looking for a clearer path back to sustainable growth and stronger profitability.

data.title: Boeing MAX 10 moves closer to certification after FAA software review
data.description:
U.S. aviation regulators have found that a software problem affecting some Boeing 737 MAX flight computers does not create a flight-safety concern, removing a regulatory obstacle to certification of the MAX 10.

A panel of safety experts at the Federal Aviation Administration concluded that the issue did not pose a safety risk because pilots continue to have full control of the aircraft and receive clear and unambiguous indications, the agency said on Friday.

The software problem can arise when a pilot abandons a landing and requires the autopilot to shift to a less automated mode for pitch control, increasing the workload for the flight crew. The FAA had paused certification of the MAX 10 earlier this week while it reviewed the issue. The agency approved the smaller MAX 7 in August despite the affected software being present.

The MAX 10, Boeing's largest 737 MAX variant, is already years behind schedule and has more than 1,500 orders. The FAA said it would assess whether any further action was necessary.

Boeing shares were trading about 2.5% higher on Friday.

data.title: GE Vernova Stocks Edges Higher as AI Power Buyers Favor Speed
data.description:
GE Vernova , the power-generation and grid-equipment company, benefited from the rush to power AI data centers, with shares edging 0.17% higher to about $989.13 at 11.44am ET as developers pursued on-site generation. The pitch is simple: secure electricity sooner and get expensive computing equipment working.

According to Reuters' reporting, Crusoe ordered 29 GE Vernova aeroderivative turbines rated at 35 megawatts apiece. That adds up to roughly 1,015 megawatts, with ten units earmarked for its Abilene AI campus. GE Vernova is also investing more than $160 million in its Greenville turbine facility. Demand is creating an opportunity, but production capacity determines how quickly orders become revenue.

Speed comes with a bill. Industry specialists told Reuters that smaller turbines can carry higher lifetime electricity costs than larger combined-cycle systems. Customers may accept that tradeoff to get online sooner. The graphic's GF Score of just 17 out of 100 adds a cautionary signal alongside the upbeat demand story. For investors, the next test is execution: turning urgent orders into deliveries, cash and durable margins.

data.title: Rockefeller Recruits $1 Billion Financial Advisor Team From Truist — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Kenneth Corbin

Rockefeller Capital Management has recruited a five-person financial advisor team from Truist Advisory Services, where it oversaw about $1 billion in client assets. The Piedmont Wealth Partners team joined Rockefeller on Wednesday, according to registration records.

Truist declined to comment on the departure.

Piedmont, based in Charlotte, N.C., includes three advisors and two support staffers. The practice caters to high- and ultrahigh-net-worth clients. The move continues Rockefeller's aggressive recruiting campaign that has drawn dozens of advisor teams in recent years.

Piedmont advisor Gavin Shuck is a 29-year industry veteran who first registered as a broker in 1997 with PaineWebber, according to the online database BrokerCheck. After a brief stint at First Union Brokerage Services he joined Wells Fargo as a broker in 2000 and registered as an investment advisor with the firm in 2001. He worked briefly at Scott & Stringfellow before joining BB&T in 2013. BB&T merged with SunTrust in 2019, and the combined entity adopted the Trust brand.

Paul Irving, another of Piedmont's advisors, has had a 28-year career as a broker. Except for his start at American Express Financial Advisors and the IDS Life Insurance Company, his career followed the same path as Shuck.

Advisor Brett Schmidt entered the industry in 2012 as a broker and advisor with BB&T.

Irving and Schmidt both hold the Certified Financial Planner credential. All three advisors are now managing directors with Rockefeller.

The team also includes support staffers Ben Beeson and Nichole McKeon.

Rockefeller sprang from the family office of oil tycoon John D. Rockefeller. The firm says it managed $237 billion in client assets as of Aug. 31.

data.title: CBOT wheat steadies near six-week low; corn and soybean futures fall
data.description:
Key points:
  • USDA's larger-than-expected US corn stocks estimate continues to weigh on corn
  • Traders await USDA crop production, monthly supply-demand reports next week
  • Early fall weather harvest delays heightening uncertainty over crop size

By P.J. Huffstutter

Chicago Board of Trade wheat futures ended nearly unchanged on Friday, hovering near six-week lows, as a Saudi Arabian import tender boosted demand sentiment even as strength in the US dollar continued to cap prices, market analysts said.

CBOT corn futures dipped lower, holding near a six-week low, as Wednesday's larger-than-expected USDA estimate of US corn stocks continued to weigh on the market. CBOT soybeans slipped under pressure from an ongoing US harvest that is projected to be hefty, and forecasts of weather improving across the central Midwest.

Questions about how big this autumn's US corn and soybean harvest will be are being hotly debated by traders, who are anxiously waiting for the US Department of Agriculture's next crop production report and its monthly World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates report next week.

Traders are eager for the government's updated forecast, as harvest across much of the Midwest has been delayed by early fall rains, said Don Roose, president of Iowa-based US Commodities.

"The fear going into that report is that USDA said the soybean yield was big in September, and that they'll say it's even bigger in the October report," Roose said. "Right now, the yield debate in the trade continues both for corn and soybeans."

On Thursday, commodity brokerage StoneX lowered its estimate of the average US 2026 corn yield and trimmed its corn production forecast, but raised soybean yield and production estimates from its previous monthly report released on September 8.

The most traded CBOT corn settled down 4-1/2 cents at $4.97-3/4 a bushel, after earlier dipping down to Thursday's six-week low of $4.95 a bushel. CBOT soybeans closed 5-3/4 cents lower at $12.78-1/4 per bushel, and CBOT wheat closed 1/4-cent higher at $6.83 per bushel.

Saudi Arabia on Thursday announced it is seeking to buy 535,000 metric tons of wheat for shipment in November and December. Traders viewed the tender as a sign that the recent price fall was stirring fresh demand after Saudi Arabia cancelled its previous wheat tender on September 7 because of high prices.

The dollar index was on track for a fourth straight weekly gain against the euro on Friday, supported by elevated US Treasury yields amid a selloff in European government bond markets and expectations the Federal Reserve will maintain its hawkish interest rate stance. US currency strength makes dollar-denominated commodities more expensive for overseas buyers.

A lack of progress in diplomatic efforts to restore normal shipping through the Black Sea also underpinned wheat prices. Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday rejected proposals for a truce in Black Sea attacks.

data.title: FAA Says 737 MAX Software Glitch Doesn't Pose Safety Issue — WSJ
data.description:
By Andrew Tangel

The Federal Aviation Administration has determined that a new Boeing 737 MAX software glitch doesn't pose a flight-safety issue, according to people familiar with the matter.

U.S. air-safety regulators had convened an internal panel known as a corrective action review board on Friday to decide whether the software glitch amounted to an unsafe condition that needed to be addressed.

"The FAA's Corrective Action Review Board made that determination because pilots retain full control of the aircraft, the indications to the flight crew are clear and unambiguous," the FAA said. "As with any situation, the FAA will consider appropriate action if it receives new information about this issue."

The glitch raised concerns among some aviation industry officials over whether it could pose a safety issue when 737 MAX jets are landing under certain circumstances, The Wall Street Journal reported.

This article will update.

data.title: U.S. Treasury Selloff Resumes After Brief Respite — 4th Update
data.description:
By Miriam Mukuru and Paulo Trevisani

Treasury yields hovered near multidecade highs Friday as investors looked past slower-than-expected job creation in the U.S. amid lingering concerns about the long-term economic outlook.

The Labor Department said a net 29,000 jobs were created in September, well below the 84,000 expected in a Wall Street Journal consensus. Past figures were revised downward by a total of 60,000 over August and July. The unemployment rate ticked higher to 4.2% from 4.1%.

The 10-year yield slipped on the morning data to an intraday low of 5.155%, before snapping back to 5.285%, close to 2007 highs reached earlier this week.

While Friday's labor numbers alleviated pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise rates for a second consecutive meeting when it convenes late this month, they didn't squelch all fears. Oil prices walked back early losses and Brent turned slightly higher, keeping inflation concerns alive.

The rise in yields is also driven by concerns about fast-rising borrowing by large AI corporations and ballooning government debt.

"Practically, this is a fiscal responsibility story," F/m Investments CEO Alex Morris said. "We have exactly zero politicians running on fiscal responsibility [and] I think that is going to be the bigger problem."

Increasing government borrowing in Europe is helping push global yields up, Morris said.

"I don't think it's as pronounced as folks are saying, but I do think there's some crowding out effect that's injuring Treasury rates," he said.

The 10-year French benchmark yield reached a 24-year high while the comparable German government-bond yields dropped sharply, before recovering some ground, LSEG data showed.

The spread between French and German 10-year sovereign bond yields jumped to its most since November 2011, reaching 158.67 basis points, up from around 84 points in September. The widening gap comes amid concerns about the French government's ability to implement budget cuts, while German debt is perceived as a safe haven.

data.title: Correction to Can AI Run in Space? Google Is About to Find Out Article on Oct. 1 — WSJ
data.description:
By Rebecca Cadenhead

Google has launched a satellite to find out whether data centers can run in space.

A prototype satellite containing four of Google's artificial-intelligence chips, called Tensor Processing Units, was launched by SpaceX on Thursday, the beginning of a year-long experiment testing whether TPUs can survive in orbit. The satellite was among several payloads loaded on a rocket that lifted off from California just after 11:30 a.m. local time.

The company hopes the project, known as Suncatcher, will someday allow it to build an orbital data center with thousands of interconnected satellites, fueled by the sun's energy. Google designed the satellite in partnership with Planet Labs. It is equipped with solar panels and will circle Earth in a sun-synchronous orbit, exposing it to sunlight around the clock.

The panels, which power the TPUs, are expected to harness up to eight times as much energy as a solar panel on Earth. The atmosphere, weather and nighttime limit how much power ground-based systems can harness.

"The sun is the biggest power source in our solar system by far," said Travis Beals, senior director of Paradigms of Intelligence, an AI research team at Google, a unit of Alphabet.

Google hopes to keep the TPUs in orbit for about a year. The chips will be used to run large language models and respond to simple queries, Beals said. The company has already exposed its TPUs to conditions that simulate space. Still, "no amount of testing is as good as the real thing," he said.

Google is one of the first companies to launch AI chips into space. Other companies, including SpaceX and Blue Origin, are planning similar projects.

News Corp, owner of The Wall Street Journal, has a commercial agreement to supply content on Google platforms.

Space-based data centers could also be suited to special use cases, said Val Elbert, global leader of Boston Consulting Group's technology, media and telecommunications practice. Governments could use these data centers to store sovereign data, and companies could use them to process satellite imagery in real-time.

Advocates for these projects have said that data centers in orbit can avoid some problems that land-based operations face including pushback from residents, land constraints and finite energy sources.

Still, space-based data centers face many challenges, from costs to radiation.

During a rocket launch, an AI chip experiences up to 100 times the force of gravity, which could damage it, Google said. Once in orbit, the chip will have to survive being bombarded by cosmic rays and solar events.

These chips could also overheat, said John Abraham, a professor of mechanical engineering at the University of St. Thomas. As AI chips process queries, they produce thermal energy. But the methods used to cool a data center on Earth don't work in orbit. Instead, space-based data centers will have to use radiators that turn heat into waves of infrared light, which are then dispersed into deep space, he said.

Google's prototype satellite is about the size of a refrigerator, the company said. But in the future, satellites will carry dozens of TPUs at a time, requiring solar panels and radiators orders of magnitude larger than the chips themselves. For example, while one TPU is a few inches wide, radiators of future satellites could be the size of a Boeing 747, said Elbert.

Beals estimates that it may take 10,000 such satellites to make a single 1-gigawatt data center in space.

That would carry an astronomically high price tag. At present, building and launching the orbital equivalent of a 1-gigawatt data center on Earth would cost around $30 billion, Elbert estimates.

Advances in launch technology will eventually make that cheaper, he added. Still, it won't entirely close the price gap with data centers on Earth.

"The cost equation will always favor Earth-based data centers," said Elbert.

Google projects that it will one day be possible to build a space-based data center as cheaply as a terrestrial data center, Beals said, though it may take years to get there.

For now, Google is waiting to see whether the TPUs it just launched into space survive undamaged, a period he said could take weeks.

"We want to see if the behavior in space matches what we saw on Earth," Beals said.

Google plans to launch more TPUs into space-this time on two interconnected satellites-in 2027.

Write to Rebecca Cadenhead at rebecca.cadenhead@wsj.com

data.title: Nigeria says domestic gas supply surpasses 2 billion cubic feet per day, eyes further growth
data.description:
By Camillus Eboh

Nigeria's domestic gas supply has crossed 2 billion cubic feet per day (bcf/d), as the government pushes to expand supplies to power plants and industries and reduce constraints on economic growth, the country's gas minister said on Friday.

  • Gas production rose to 7.5 bcf/d from about 6.8 bcf/d in 2023, Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Gas) Ekperikpe Ekpo said. Proven gas reserves have increased to 215.19 trillion cubic feet (tcf) from 208.83 tcf, Ekpo said.

  • Nigeria is targeting gas production of 10 bcf/d by 2027 and 12 bcf/d by 2030 to meet growing demand from power generation, industry, fertiliser production, petrochemicals, liquefied natural gas (LNG), transportation and export markets.

  • To support higher domestic supply, the Obiafu-Obrikom-Oben (OB3) pipeline has reached full completion and is being prepared for first gas, Ekpo said. The pipeline can transport 2 bcf/d and is expected to unlock more than 500 million standard cubic feet per day (MMscf/d) of additional gas for the domestic market.

  • The Ajaokuta-Kaduna-Kano (AKK) pipeline is about 95% complete, he added.

  • Ekpo said 671 billion naira ($434 million) deployed through the Midstream and Downstream Gas Infrastructure Fund had attracted about 1.6 trillion naira in private investment across 31 projects and 205 infrastructure assets.

  • The projects are expected to deliver about 475 MMscf/d to the domestic market when fully operational. Nigeria is targeting about $30 billion in gas-sector investment by 2030.

data.title: Apple updates Full Disk Access controls in macOS in response to probing AI agents
data.description:
Apple plans to update its controls regarding "Full Disk Access" in macOS in response to artificial intelligence agents potentially probing all available avenues of user data.

The Cupertino-based company warned that developers using "Full Disk Access" can expose everything on their systems to personal AI agents, including files, mail, private messages and browsing history. This not only creates potential privacy issues for the user but also for those a user communicates with.

"Going forward, we will introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action," Apple said in a developer update on Friday. "Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy."

The update follows potential concerns over Meta's Muse app. Last month, tech columnist Jason Aten wrote a piece for Inc. that his Muse AI agent was reviewing his private messages and emails even though he had not given it permission to do so.

In one example, he said Muse sent him a push notification suggesting that a text message conversation he was having with his co-host would make for a good column. It even offered to start researching the topic. It also flagged another private message he had exchanged with his editor days prior about the proposed column's due date.

"Not only had I not asked it to do that sort of thing, I never gave it permission to read my messages," Aten wrote. "In fact, I remember explicitly choosing not to let it have access to my messages, calendar, and other personal information."
